newsitem.title: UK: Ireland gives London dossier on disputed killings.
newsitem.headline: Ireland gives London dossier on disputed killings.

text.p: Ireland gave Britain a dossier about "Bloody Sunday" on Tuesday, one of the most controversial episodes in recent Anglo-Irish history when 13 unarmed Catholics were shot dead by British troops, and urged London to exonerate the victims.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told his British counterpart Tony Blair that London had the opportunity to heal old wounds and help the Northern Ireland peace efforts by establishing the truth of the paratroops' killings in the province's second city, Londonderry.
The dossier, containing the Irish government's assessment of recent new evidence about the incident, was handed over by Irish civil servants to British officials in Belfast.

The shootings and a subsequent official inquiry, which held that British paratroopers were fired on first, has been a running sore in Anglo-Irish relations. Nationalists have made repeated calls for a new inquiry to clear the victims.
The January 30, 1972 killings took place in the early stages of a guerrilla war against British rule, a conflict that has claimed more than 3,200 lives.
They fuelled nationalist mistrust of Britain and were blamed for disaffected young Catholics joining guerrilla Irish Republican Army, which opposes rule by Britain.

Bruton said the emergence of the new evidence had added weight to the view that a new inquiry was needed and said he welcomed indications by Tony Blair's Labour Government that it would take a fresh look at the killings.
"There is now an opportunity to lay to rest this most troubling and distrubing episode of the terrible history of the past 27 years," Bruton said.

Relatives of Catholics who were shot on "Bloody Sunday", during an illegal protest march, have campaigned for the overturning of the official report, conducted by the then Chief Justice, Lord Widgery. They said it smeared the reputations of those who died.
Widgery said that some of the army firing "bordered on the reckless" and that none of the dead or wounded had been proven to have been handling weapons or bombs when hit.
New evidence last year pointed to the possibility that some were killed by previously unrecorded shots by other non-paratroop soldiers.

Bruton, in a letter to Prime Minister Blair said Ireland welcomed the acknowledgement by his predecessor John Major that the victims should be regarded as innocent of any allegation that they were shot while handling firearms of explosives.

"In the light of the Assessment, the victims of Bloody Sunday were a unique group in that the injustice of their fate -- at the hands of those whose duty it was to respect as well as to uphold the rule of law -- was compounded by a second injustice arising directly from the Widgery Report," Bruton wrote.
"I believe that your approach on this issue can help remove a source of profound distress not only to the relatives but to the nationalist community generally."
